title: The binding of Isaac (Genesis 22)
hook: the hardest story in Genesis; Jewish readers have argued over it for two thousand years

segments.voice: Yesterday: Hagar and Ishmael in the desert, and God opened her eyes. Your line was the well was there. Did you find one? Today is a hard story. Day forty-eight.

In the old JPS translation it begins: "God did prove Abraham." God calls his name, and Abraham answers with one Hebrew word, hineni: here I am. Then the command, slow and piling up, each phrase heavier than the last: "Take now thy son, thine only son, whom thou lovest, even Isaac." Take him to the land of Moriah, and offer him there on a mountain. This is the son Sarah laughed about. The son of the promise, the stars, the whole future. Abraham gets up early. He saddles his donkey, splits the wood, and walks for three days. The Torah tells us nothing about what he feels. Nothing. Jewish readers have argued over this story for a very long time. Today, we don't settle it either.
screen: `GOD DID PROVE ABRAHAM.` → `HINENI — HERE I AM.` → `THINE ONLY SON, WHOM THOU LOVEST.`

segments.voice: On the third day, father and son walk up the mountain alone, Isaac carrying the wood. And Isaac speaks, the only time he does in this story: my father, he says, and then: "Behold the fire and the wood; but where is the lamb for a burnt-offering?" Abraham answers: "God will provide Himself the lamb for a burnt-offering, my son." And the Torah says: they went both of them together. Abraham builds the altar, binds Isaac, and lifts the knife. And an angel calls: Abraham, Abraham. Hineni, again. "Lay not thy hand upon the lad." He sees a ram caught by its horns in a thicket, and offers it instead. Jews call this the Akedah, the binding, from the verb in the verse, because Isaac was bound, and not sacrificed. And here is where the tradition wrestles. Some read it as the peak of devotion: a man ready to give everything. It's read on Rosh Hashanah, and the Talmud connects the ram's horn, the shofar, to this ram. Others read the ending as the point: God stops the knife, and they hear the Torah saying no to child sacrifice. Others feel the silence. The same Abraham who argued with God for the strangers of Sodom says nothing for his own son. The very next chapter opens with Sarah's death, and a midrash says she died when she heard what had happened. And when Abraham walks down the mountain, the verse mentions only him. Where is Isaac? The Torah doesn't say. None of these readings cancels the others. The tradition keeps them all, and keeps asking.
screen: `WHERE IS THE LAMB?` · `LAY NOT THY HAND UPON THE LAD.` · `AKEDAH — THE BINDING.` · `DEVOTION, A NO, OR A SILENCE?` · then, large: `THEY WENT BOTH OF THEM TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one question you can't resolve. About this story, maybe, or about your own life: a loss that doesn't make sense, a choice you still can't judge, something about God or the world that doesn't add up. Don't try to answer it. Just let it sit with you, the way the tradition lets this story sit, year after year. Breathe beside it. If you pray, you can bring the question itself into your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Akedah. The binding of Isaac. A hard story in Genesis, and one the tradition keeps reading, and arguing with.
Your line: the tradition wrestles here. Today, let one hard question stay a question, without forcing an answer. Day forty-eight.

howItsDone: Jews read the Akedah on the second day of Rosh Hashanah, when the shofar, a ram's horn, recalls the ram; many prayer books also include it in the daily morning service.

what it means: the binding, read as devotion, as God's no to child sacrifice, and as a painful silence, all at once.
what a scholar hears: 22:19 names only Abraham coming down the mountain, and the midrash asks where Isaac went; Rosh Hashanah 16a links the shofar to the ram.

notes: Confirm JPS 1917 wording of Genesis 22:1 ('God did prove Abraham'), 22:2, 22:7, 22:8 and 22:12.

Sensitive: the hardest story in Genesis. Three readings are given without ranking (devotion; rejection of child sacrifice; the troubling silence). Keeper to confirm balance and whether any major reading is missing.
Sarah's death on hearing of the Akedah: Rashi on 23:2 (from Genesis Rabbah 58:5 / Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer 32). Confirm.
Isaac's absence in 22:19 and midrashic answers (e.g. sent to study with Shem): only the question is raised.
Rosh Hashanah 16a: blow a ram's horn so that I remember the binding of Isaac. Confirm. Akedah read on the second day of Rosh Hashanah; recited daily in many siddurim. Confirm.
